summary: This informational memo gives proposed registration and administration procedures for Chinese domain names. Many common Chinese characters have variants, so most names have at least two forms, and equivalence between Simplified and Traditional Chinese is key. It builds on RFC 3743 and explains the IANA tables.

plainLanguage.summary: Some Chinese characters can be written in more than one way. This explains how a website name can be reserved in all its spellings so nobody steals the twin.

questions: simplified and traditional chinese domain names
subtitle: Registering Chinese domain names that have variants in both Simplified and Traditional forms

tldr.problem: Chinese characters have two major forms: Simplified (used in mainland China) and Traditional (used in Taiwan and elsewhere). A single domain name often has multiple valid spellings. Without a consistent registration approach, domain name registration becomes confusing and opens the possibility of different spellings being registered to different parties.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC provides specific registration procedures based on RFC 3743 (the JET Guidelines for CJK domain names). It defines Simplified Chinese Variant Table (SCVT) and Traditional Chinese Variant Table (TCVT), which list which characters are variants of each other. The procedure ensures that when a domain name is registered, both Simplified and Traditional forms are included as equivalents.
tldr.outcome: Domain registry operators (like CNNIC for .CN and TWNIC for .TW) can now apply consistent rules that prevent confusion and allow users to access a registered name using either character form, improving accessibility of Chinese-language internet resources.

today: RFC 4713 is an Informational document and has not been obsoleted. The registration and administration procedures it recommends remain in use by the CNNIC and TWNIC registries for managing Chinese domain names with variant character forms.

sections.title: The Challenge of Chinese Character Variants
sections.content:
With Internationalized Domain Names (IDNs), domain names can now contain non-ASCII characters, allowing users to access the Internet in their native languages. However, many languages have special challenges beyond basic character support.

Chinese presents a unique problem: many common characters have two forms. During the 20th century, the Chinese character set was simplified to make reading and writing easier. These Simplified characters have been adopted in mainland China and Singapore, while Traditional forms remain in use in Taiwan, Hong Kong, and many overseas communities. When both forms are used globally on the Internet, significant confusion can arise if the two forms are not treated as variants of each other.

This RFC builds on RFC 3743 (the JET Guidelines for CJK domain names) to provide specific procedures for registering and managing Chinese domain names. It explains how the CNNIC (registry for .CN) and TWNIC (registry for .TW) have deployed systems to handle Simplified and Traditional character equivalence.
sections.plainLanguage: One Chinese word can be written in two ways. If a website name can only be registered one way, people using the other spelling won't find it. This explains how to register it both ways.

sections.title: Character Variants and Domain Name Registration
sections.content:
A Chinese Domain Name Label (CDNL) is an IDN label that includes at least one Chinese character. It may also contain standard letters, digits, and hyphens.

The RFC defines two variant tables, both based on RFC 3743's framework:

  • Simplified Chinese Variant Table (SCVT): Lists character variants where the preferred form is the Simplified character used by mainland Chinese or defined in Chinese standards.
  • Traditional Chinese Variant Table (TCVT): Lists variants where the preferred form is the Traditional character used in Taiwan or related standards.

When a user submits a domain name for registration (the Original Chinese Domain Name Label, or OCDNL), the registration procedure applies these tables to generate additional forms. The result is that a single submitted name can generate up to three records: the original, the Simplified form, and the Traditional form. The procedure ensures these are proper variants and does not create names with mixed Simplified and Traditional characters.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two lists: one that says which characters are simplified and one that says which are traditional. When you register a domain, the system looks at both lists and adds all the matching variants.

sections.title: How Domain Names Are Registered
sections.content:
The registration procedure follows the RFC 3743 framework, using terminology like "character variants" (CV) and "preferred variants" (PV). When processing an input character against the Simplified Chinese variant table, the system produces the Simplified preferred variant; when processing against the Traditional table, it produces the Traditional preferred variant.

The first columns of the SCVT and TCVT are identical, as are their third columns. This ensures that the character variants computed for a given input character are the same regardless of which table is consulted. The PV (preferred variant) differs: SCVT prefers Simplified forms, while TCVT prefers Traditional forms.

A registry may optionally apply additional rules to reduce the number of variant labels added to the zone file. For example, a registry could require that the original submitted name be in only Simplified or only Traditional form, and use that as the preferred variant if the algorithm would generate multiple options. Some registries might use artificial intelligence or feedback from registrants to ensure that generated variants make linguistic sense.
sections.plainLanguage: The computer processes the name through both tables. It creates the simplified version and the traditional version. Sometimes it might skip some combinations if they don't make sense as real words.

sections.title: Security Implications of Variant Handling
sections.content:
This document addresses the same security considerations as RFC 3743. One key security goal is to reduce the potential for confusion and fraud. Some Chinese characters look very similar but have different meanings—visual similarity can be exploited for phishing attacks or domain name hijacking.

By treating Simplified and Traditional variants as equivalent during registration, this system reduces one major source of confusion. It prevents a scenario where a legitimate business has registered a domain in Traditional characters while an attacker registers an apparently similar name using Simplified characters, potentially deceiving users.

However, the RFC acknowledges that the relationship between variants is contextual: whether one character can substitute for another sometimes depends on the other characters around it in the label. Registries may need to apply additional rules or human review to ensure that generated variant labels are plausible and legitimate.
sections.plainLanguage: Registering both forms of a name together prevents scammers from registering a look-alike using the other script. It makes the system more secure for everyone.

sections.title: Understanding the Variant Tables
sections.content:
The RFC defines specific terminology based on RFC 3743. The Simplified Chinese Variant Table and Traditional Chinese Variant Table are published as IANA IDN Languages Tables and are referenced as [LVT-SC] and [LVT-TC].

The variant tables follow the structure and terminologies defined in RFC 3743, including the concept of zone variants (ZV)—preferred variants that are eligible for inclusion in the DNS zone file. These tables define which characters are valid for use in Chinese domain names and which forms are preferred by each table.

The document emphasizes that a complete understanding of RFC 3743 is necessary for properly implementing these tables. The tables themselves are not normative specifications but rather tools for registries to apply the JET Guidelines specifically to Chinese characters.
sections.plainLanguage: There are official lists that show which characters are simplified and which are traditional, and how they map to each other. These lists are used by the domain registries in China and Taiwan.
